segments.say: Lesson 2. Big-O & Complexity. Count the work, not the seconds. O of 1 to O of 2 to the n, with how to read constraints and pick the target complexity.

Big-O describes how the amount of work grows as the input gets bigger. It's not seconds, it's the shape of growth: flat, slowly rising, straight line, or exploding. Here is an analogy. Finding a friend's name: checking every page of a phone book is O of n. Opening the middle and halving each time is O of log n. Being told the exact page number is O of 1.

Why does this matter? Every interview answer ends with "time is O of., space is O of. ". The input size in the constraints tells you which complexity you need, which tells you which pattern to use. A few key words. n: The size of the input (number of elements). Time complexity: How the number of steps grows with n. Space complexity: How much extra memory grows with n. O of 1: Constant: same work for any n. O of n: Linear: one pass over the data. O of n squared: Quadratic: every pair, nested loops.
Operations for n equals 8. O of 1: same work no matter how big the input is. Array index, hash map get/set (on average).
O of log n: cut the problem in half each step. n equals 1,000,000 leads to only ~20 steps.
O of n: one pass. Most two-pointer, sliding-window and hash map solutions.
O of n log n: efficient sorting (merge sort, Timsort in Python's sort() ), and heap operations over n items.
O of n squared: nested loops over the input. The usual brute force. n equals 10 to the 5, giving 10 to the 10 operations, way too slow.
O of 2 to the n or O of n!: all subsets or permutations (backtracking). Only OK for n less than or equal to ~20.

Read the constraints to guess the intended solution. n less than or equal to 20 leads to O of 2 to the n backtracking is fine. n less than or equal to 1,000 leads to O of n squared is OK. n less than or equal to 10 to the 5–10 to the 6 leads to need O of n log n or O of n. n less than or equal to 10 to the 9 (or values that large) leads to O of log n or math. Think binary search on the answer. A rule of thumb: ~10 to the 8 simple operations per second.

Rules for computing Big-O. Drop constants: O of 2n equals O of n. Keep the dominant term: O of n squared plus n equals O of n squared. Sequential steps add; nested steps multiply. Different inputs get different variables: O of n plus m, O of n, m. Space complexity counts extra memory: hash maps, recursion stack depth.

Python costs to know. list.append, pop() from end: O of 1. pop(0) / insert(0,x): O of n, so use collections.deck. x in list: O of n. x in set / dict: O of 1 average. Slicing a i:j copies: O of j minus i. String concatenation in a loop: O of n squared, so use ''.join(). sorted(): O of n log n. heap Q.heappush/pop: O of log n.

Say it in the interview. "The brute force checks every pair, which is O of n squared. With n up to 10 to the 5 that's too slow, so I'll aim for O of n using a hash map to trade O of n extra space for constant-time lookups.".

Let's compare. O of 1: 1, hash lookup, math. O of log n: ~17, binary search, balanced tree. O of n: 10 to the 5, single pass, two pointers, sliding window. O of n log n: ~1.7 times 10 to the 6, sort plus scan, heap. O of n squared: 10 to the 10, nested loops, simple D P on pairs. O of 2 to the n: ∞, subsets, backtracking (small n only).

A likely interview question: How do you pick an approach from constraints? A strong answer: Map n to an allowed complexity: less than or equal to 20 leads to exponential, less than or equal to 10 cubed leads to n squared, less than or equal to 10 to the 5–10 to the 6 leads to n log n or n, huge leads to log n or math. Then pick the pattern that achieves it.
That's it for Big-O & Complexity. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
